hints: Look closely at the shape of layer Y in P versus Q. Which leaf is flat and open, and which one has rolled up into a C-shape after 45 minutes?
Remember how hinge or motor cells in a xerophytic leaf control rolling. What does loss of turgor in the upper layer Y do to water potential and to net water movement after time for equilibrium?
walkthrough:
**Observe what P and Q show**

Look at the outline. In P the leaf is flat and open. In Q the leaf has curled inwards with layer Y on the inside of the curl.

This curling is the classic xerophyte response to water loss.

**Link shape to turgor in layer Y**

Layer Y acts like hinge cells. When they take up water they are turgid and push the leaf flat, that is P.

When they lose water they become flaccid and may plasmolyse, so the leaf rolls up, that is Q. So statement 2 is true and statement 3, which says the opposite, is false.

**Link turgor to water potential**

More water in cells means higher, less negative, water potential.

$$ \text{P (turgid, more water) has higher } \Psi \text{ than Q (flaccid, less water)} $$
So statement 1 is true: less negative in P than in Q.

**Think about net movement after 45 minutes**

45 minutes is a long time. The cells have had time to come to equilibrium with their surroundings.

At equilibrium there is no further net diffusion of water into Y in either condition. So statement 4 is true. That gives 1, 2 and 4, which is option A.

options.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are all true. P is turgid with higher water potential, Q is flaccid with lower water potential, and both are at equilibrium after 45 minutes.
options.B: Incorrect. It correctly includes 1 and 4 but wrongly includes 3. Cells are more turgid in flat P, not less turgid than in rolled Q.
options.C: Incorrect. It includes 1 but also includes false statement 3, and it misses true statements 2 and 4.
options.D: Incorrect. It includes true statements 2 and 4 but misses true statement 1 about less negative water potential in P.
